prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s dark in here, the dark inside of a man in the dark. It’s not night. One hears crows overhead, dawn fowl caws, the shod soles again treading their sunlit plots above. One grows dotish-fond of such things. Long live the things, their ways, their roots pushed goatish & gray through the skull, in this earth that gaily spins though one has crossed its smutted green threshold to reign in a crate. We have done no wrong, my friends, & yet we find ourselves soiled, sold, carbonized teeth in a moss-riven jaw. Once I sat on a stool as my grandmother told me of heaven. She cleaned fish for our living. I saw how her rusty black knife unseamed the sunset in each belly—coral, ochre, carmine, raw, lice-infested sunsets in a pail. So many nights. Night in the kitchen shack, night at the crumbling edge of our milk-pond province, a blade, lone cricket raving in the lawn.

prompts.L3:

- The speaker describes an oppressive darkness that feels like being buried or confined beneath the living world.
- Sounds of crows, dawn birds, and footsteps above emphasize the speaker’s separation from ordinary life.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, Long, Once

outputs.L1:
It is dark in here: the darkness inside a man in the dark. It is not night. One hears crows overhead—dawn-fowl caws—the shod soles once again treading their sunlit plots above. One grows dotish-fond of such things. Long live the things: their ways, their roots pushed goatish and gray through the skull, in this earth that spins so gaily, though one has crossed its smutted green threshold to reign in a crate. We have done no wrong, my friends, and yet we find ourselves soiled, sold, carbonized teeth in a moss-riven jaw.

Once, I sat on a stool as my grandmother told me of heaven. She cleaned fish for our living. I saw how her rusty black knife unseamed the sunset in each belly—coral, ochre, carmine, raw, lice-infested sunsets in a pail. So many nights. Night in the kitchen shack; night at the crumbling edge of our milk-pond province; a blade; a lone cricket raving in the lawn.
outputs.L2:
It is dim here—the kind of darkness that belongs to a man enclosed in darkness. Yet it is not nighttime. Above, crows can be heard, the cries of birds at daybreak, and once more the nailed soles of shoes crossing their bright parcels of ground overhead. A person becomes foolishly tender toward such things. Let those things endure—their habits, their roots, gray and goatlike, thrusting through the skull, in this world that keeps spinning cheerfully even after one has stepped past its stained green border to rule from a box. We have committed no offense, my friends, and still we end up dirtied, bartered away, like blackened teeth set in a jaw split with moss.

There was a time I sat on a stool while my grandmother spoke to me about heaven. She gutted fish to keep us alive. I watched her dark, rusted knife open the evening light hidden in each belly—coral, ocher, crimson, raw sunsets crawling with lice and dropped into a bucket. So many nights: night inside the kitchen hut, night along the collapsing rim of our milky-pond region, a knife nearby, and a single cricket shrieking madly in the grass.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents a world dominated by oppressive darkness, creating the feeling of being buried, trapped, or confined beneath the surface of ordinary life. This darkness is not only physical but emotional and psychological, suggesting a state of isolation, fear, and suffering. The speaker seems cut off from the living world above, as though they exist in a hidden or forgotten place where light and freedom cannot reach.

This sense of separation is strengthened by the sounds the speaker hears. The cries of crows, the calls of birds at dawn, and the footsteps passing overhead all remind the speaker that life continues elsewhere. These sounds belong to the ordinary world of movement, morning, and human activity, but the speaker can only experience them from a distance. Rather than offering comfort, they emphasize the speaker’s confinement and exclusion. The world above is alive, while the speaker remains trapped below it.

The speaker also reflects on innocence and suffering. There is a strong suggestion that they, and perhaps others like them, have been punished or harmed despite having done nothing wrong. This creates a feeling of injustice at the heart of the text. The speaker’s suffering is not presented as deserved, but as something imposed upon the innocent. This reflection broadens the poem’s meaning, turning a personal experience into a larger meditation on cruelty, victimhood, and the ways people can be wronged by forces beyond their control.

A vivid memory of the speaker’s grandmother cleaning fish adds another layer to the text. This image connects family life and survival with death and violence. Cleaning fish may be an ordinary domestic task, associated with nourishment and care, but it is also filled with images of blood, bodies, and exposure. Through this memory, the speaker links the intimate world of family with the harsher realities of life and death. The grandmother’s action becomes both practical and symbolic, showing how survival often depends on confronting death directly.

Throughout the text, there is a powerful contrast between natural beauty and images of decay, violence, and confinement. Birds, dawn, and the living world suggest freedom and renewal, yet they are placed beside darkness, burial, death, and suffering. This contrast makes the speaker’s situation feel even more painful. Nature is present, but it does not fully rescue or comfort the speaker. Instead, beauty and brutality exist side by side, creating a tense and haunting atmosphere. The result is a text that explores confinement, innocence, memory, and survival through a mixture of delicate natural imagery and disturbing images of violence and decay.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a haunting meditation on confinement, death, and undeserved suffering. It builds its meaning through dense, surreal imagery in which the speaker seems trapped below the surface of the world, surrounded by darkness, decay, roots, and the pressure of the earth. This underground space suggests imprisonment, burial, and social abandonment all at once. Yet the darkness is not silent. From above come signs of continuing life: the calls of crows, the movement of people, the distant presence of sunlight, weather, and ordinary human activity. The contrast between the buried speaker and the living world overhead intensifies the sense of injustice, as though life continues indifferently while some are forced to endure pain, exclusion, or premature death.

Memory deepens this vision. The recollection of a grandmother cleaning fish introduces an image that is both domestic and violent. The knife, the fish, the blood, and the practiced motions of the grandmother connect everyday survival with death. What might seem like a simple household memory becomes charged with symbolic force: the body is vulnerable, life is easily cut open, and nourishment is inseparable from killing. In this way, ordinary sensory details become unsettling reminders of mortality.

The text’s power comes from the way it refuses to separate beauty from degradation. Crows, roots, knives, sunsets, fish, and soil are not merely decorative images; they carry the emotional weight of memory, suffering, and injustice. The world it describes is harsh and often cruel, but it is also intensely alive. Even in confinement, the senses remain active. Sounds, colors, smells, and remembered gestures continue to press into consciousness. As a result, human existence appears both diminished and vivid: people may be trapped, harmed, or forgotten, yet their inner lives remain crowded with sensation, memory, and meaning.

Ultimately, the text transforms physical images into a larger vision of the human condition. It suggests that suffering is often undeserved and that death is always close to ordinary life. At the same time, it shows that even degraded existence contains flashes of beauty and vitality. The result is a disturbing but powerful portrait of life under the shadow of mortality, where the smallest details of the world become symbols of endurance, loss, and injustice.
outputs.L5:
Once, there was one long road that stretched beyond the hills and disappeared into the quiet horizon. Travelers spoke of it as a path of patience, because no one could reach its end in a single day. Along the way, people discovered small villages, bright rivers, and moments of peace they had never expected.

One traveler decided to follow the long road without rushing. Once he stopped counting the miles, he began to notice the beauty around him: the sound of birds, the warmth of the sun, and the kindness of strangers. By the time he reached his destination, he understood that the journey had changed him more than the arrival ever could.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, gothic prose poem in the voice of a dead man buried underground, with imagery of crows, roots, fish-gutting, childhood memory, and a grandmother describing heaven.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the black arithmetic of crows, I lie where the rain is translated into wormwork and root-script, where every oak above me writes its hunger through my ribs. I am the buried man, the loosened button, the mouth packed shut with ancestral clay. In the dark I hear the village turning its knives against the bellies of fish: the silver rip, the wet alphabet of entrails, the thumb scooping out what once meant swimming. How clean the living make a death when it is not their own.

Roots finger my pockets for coins. Roots comb my hair. Roots enter me tenderly as children entering a forbidden room.

Once I was small and ran barefoot beside the ditch where minnows trembled like torn foil, and the crows came down in their priest-black coats to inspect the world’s leftovers. My grandmother sat on the porch with her hands folded over each other like two pale moths, telling me heaven was a white kitchen where no one hungered, where my grandfather waited with his cap in his hands, where every sorrow would be washed and set to dry in the sun. She said the dead rose light as bread. She said the Lord kept rooms for us.

But here there are no rooms, only pressure; no white kitchen, only this red memory of apples, this mud closing over my ears. The crows above argue over the weather in cracked Latin. The roots, blind and patient, pull me upward grain by grain. I dream of my grandmother’s heaven and smell instead the fishmonger’s bucket, scales shining like lost stars, guts steaming in the morning cold.

If I rise, it will not be as bread. It will be as nettle, as crow-feather, as the bitter green tongue of grass pushing through the churchyard, whispering to the shoes of mourners: I was a child once. I was promised light. I remember everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary passage that sounds like experimental Southern Gothic fiction: first-person plural, claustrophobic, earthy, surreal, with someone reflecting from inside a coffin or grave.
counterfactuals.output:
We have been down here long enough for the roots to learn our names.

They come nosing through the dark like pale fingers, like the hands of children feeling under a door for a dropped coin. They stroke the lid above us, worry the seams, sip at the damp where our breath used to be. Sometimes we believe they are kin. Sometimes we believe they are the town itself, reaching after us with its buried thirst, its church bells gone green with mildew, its women in flour-sack dresses whispering over hot stoves, its men spitting tobacco into the dust and calling that prayer.

The coffin is narrower than memory.

We lie shoulder to shoulder with ourselves, though there is only the one body, or what remains persuaded to keep its shape. We say we because no one ever came to this earth alone. Our mother’s crying is packed in here with us. Our father’s silence. The mule’s bad eye. The summer the creek boiled up with frogs and the preacher said it was a sign, though of what he would not say. The house with its porch sagging like a jaw. The red clay under our nails. The taste of pennies. The storm that lifted the roof clean off the smokehouse and set it down in the road like a hat.

All of it is in here, pressed close, sweating.

Above us, the county continues its old tricks. Rain fattens the grave. Sun bakes it hard. Beetles make their black parades. The living walk over us in their polished shoes and do not know how loud they are. Every footfall blooms in our teeth. Every hymn comes down warped, as if sung through a mouthful of mud. On Sundays the cemetery fills with perfume, cut grass, lies. They stand beside our stone and say we are resting.

We are not resting.

We are listening.

We hear the dead in neighboring boxes turning their stories over and over until the stories shine like bones. Miss Ada, who swallowed lye and blamed the Lord. The twins who drowned in the cistern, still arguing which one pushed. Old Mr. Voss, buried with his watch, cursing time for continuing without him. At night we all murmur together, a low wet congregation, while the worms thread us into the common tongue.

There are dreams even here. Not sleep, no. Something deeper and less merciful. We dream of standing in the kitchen again, barefoot on the cool boards, while something with our grandmother’s face fries okra in a skillet full of river water. We dream of the moon laying eggs in the cotton field. We dream the coffin opens not upward but inward, and inside that inwardness is another town, smaller, meaner, built entirely of our mistakes.

In that town, we are always almost forgiven.

But then the dirt settles its weight against us, firm as a hand on the chest, and the dark comes back whole. We remember the last light: a strip of sky, white as a peeled onion, and faces leaning over us, already receding, already practicing how to speak of us in the past tense. Someone dropped a clod of earth onto the lid. It struck like a judge’s gavel. Then another. Then the whole world began to bury us, eager, shovelful by shovelful, as if it had been waiting all along.

Now the boards soften. The satin rots to lace. Our bones grow intimate with the clay. We are being taken apart so slowly it feels like being understood.

And still, somewhere above, the old house stands with its windows blind and its chimney full of swallows. Still the road runs past the cemetery toward the swamp. Still the living carry their secrets in covered dishes, still they lower their eyes at the mention of our name, still they pretend the ground is solid beneath them.

We know better.

We are the ground now.

We hold them up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark poetic monologue about being buried alive or dead, mixing grave imagery with memories of poverty, a grandmother cleaning fish, and strange religious overtones.
counterfactuals.output:
I woke beneath the earth—  
or dreamed I woke—  
with a mouth full of dark and the weight of the world  
pressing its black thumb to my tongue.

Above me, the roots were whispering their little prayers,  
thin fingers of trees feeling for my face  
as if I were a coin dropped in the mud.  
The coffin boards sweated.  
The worms moved like priests in their soft vestments,  
blind and patient,  
coming to take communion from me.

I could not tell if I was buried alive  
or merely dead enough to remember.

I remembered the old house first—  
not as a house, but as a hunger with windows.  
The roof leaked when it rained,  
and in winter the walls held cold the way a beggar holds a cup.  
We had soup thin enough to read scripture through.  
We had shoes with mouths at the toes.  
We had laughter sometimes,  
but it sounded embarrassed to be there.

My grandmother stood at the sink  
with a fish in her hands,  
silver and trembling though it was already gone.  
She scraped the scales with the back of a knife,  
and they flew like little moons against the basin.  
Her hands were brown, cracked, holy—  
hands that had buried babies, kneaded bread,  
wrung chickens’ necks, folded napkins for men  
who never learned her name.

She slit the fish open from throat to tail  
with the calm of an angel performing judgment.  
Inside: red thread, pearl organs,  
the secret wet alphabet of survival.  
She would rinse it clean beneath the faucet  
and hum a hymn with no mercy in it.

“God provides,” she used to say,  
while the cupboards answered with their emptiness.

Now I lie here provided for at last—  
a room the exact size of my body,  
a door that does not open,  
a pillow of dirt,  
a ceiling of sod.  
The rich go upward in stories,  
in white marble and polished names,  
but the poor go down plainly,  
returned without ceremony to the landlord earth.

Somewhere above me, rain begins.  
I hear it knocking on the grave  
like fingers on a table where no food is served.  
The soil drinks.  
The roses bow their red heads,  
fat as wounds.  
A church bell rings and rings,  
not calling me back,  
only counting what has already been taken.

And yet—  
in this pit, this wooden lung,  
I feel the old religion stirring.

Not the clean one from Sunday walls,  
not the blue-eyed saint with his gentle hands,  
but the God of gutting knives and river mud,  
the God who lives in fish blood,  
in stale bread,  
in grandmothers bent over sinks,  
in the steam rising from a poor man’s supper  
like the soul leaving without complaint.

Maybe resurrection is not a trumpet.  
Maybe it is not light breaking the stone.  
Maybe it is a woman in an apron  
cleaning what can be cleaned,  
saving what can be saved,  
throwing the useless parts to the cats.

Maybe heaven smells of salt and scales.

Maybe the angels have cracked knuckles.

Maybe I am only a fish on the Lord’s table,  
opened by the dark,  
washed by the rain,  
waiting for some terrible hand  
to lift me shining from myself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, archaic, unsettling paragraph in the style of a modernist prose poem, using rich color imagery and themes of death, soil, family, and innocence.
counterfactuals.output: Beneath the violet hush of evening, where the black loam breathes like a widowed beast, the child went softly among the graves, carrying in her milk-white hands a posy of bruised marigolds and bluebells pale as drowned eyes. O mother, O father, ye lay there in the red-brown earth, folded into roots and rain, while the house upon the hill kept its yellow windows open like old wounds. The worms made scripture of your names; the clay took your laughter and darkened it. Yet she, little lamb of ash and April, knew not the terror of the furrow, nor how all kin are gathered at last into the same cold cradle. She sang to the nettles, and the nettles bowed; she kissed the stone, and the stone was mute. Around her the dusk grew green, then purple, then the deep imperial black of funeral cloth, and still her small voice wandered, innocent and thin, over that hungry soil which had eaten the family whole and waited, patient as God, for her.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a macabre first-person narration from beneath the earth, where the speaker hears life continuing above and recalls a childhood scene involving fish, sunset colors, and talk of heaven.
counterfactuals.output:
Beneath the earth, sound comes down softened, as if the world above has wrapped itself in wool.

Footsteps pass over me. Heavy ones, light ones. The uncertain patter of a child who has not yet learned that the ground keeps secrets. Wheels grind along the road beyond the cemetery wall; rain needles the grass and seeps, cold and patient, through the packed soil. In spring, roots worry at my box with the delicate insistence of fingers. In summer, beetles click in the dark like tiny teeth. Life goes on overhead, vulgar and bright, shaking crumbs from its table onto my grave.

Sometimes I hear laughter.

That is the worst of it.

Not the worms, though they have made a parliament of me. Not the dark, which is no longer dark to one who has become its citizen. Not the slow loosening of myself—the jaw unhinged from speech, the ribs opening like a ruined gate. It is the laughter, rising and falling above me, that reminds me the world has not paused even for an hour.

A dog barks. A woman calls a name. Wind drags dry leaves across my stone, and their scraping becomes, in my mind, the sound of scales.

I am a child again.

We are at the river at evening, my father and I, with a tin pail between us. The fish inside it flash and buck, silver coins tossed by a nervous god. Their mouths open and close, open and close, as if they are trying to tell us what waits below the surface.

The sun is dying magnificently. I remember the colors with an ache more vivid than flesh: orange poured like hot metal across the water, pink clouds fraying into violet, the west bruised purple at the edges. My father holds up one of the fish, and its scales catch the whole burning sky. For a moment it seems not dead or dying, but made of sunset.

“Do fish go to heaven?” I ask him.

He laughs, not cruelly. I can still hear that laugh through the dirt.

“If there’s a heaven worth having,” he says, “there’ll be rivers in it.”

“And fish?”

“Fish, and your mother’s blue bowl, and bread still warm from the oven.”

I believed him. Children believe the dead are only people who have walked ahead and found better rooms. I pictured heaven as a place full of water and evening light, where nothing gasped, where every hook came free, where my mother stood whole and smiling with flour on her hands.

Now I lie beneath a narrow garden of weeds, and the rain filters down tasting of iron.

Above me, someone kneels. I hear the creak of leather, the wet pull of breath. A hand brushes dirt from my name. For a moment, I think they might dig. Foolish hope—old reflex of bone. But no. They only leave flowers. Their stems are cut; their heads are bright; they are already dying.

The living are fond of such gestures.

They lower beauty toward us in little offerings, never understanding how quickly everything joins us. Petal, coffin, cheek, root, rib. The earth receives all colors and makes of them one color in the end.

Still, when sunset comes, I know it.

Even here.

The warmth fades first from the upper soil, then from the stones, then from the deep places where I keep my long watch. The insects quiet. The roots hold still. Somewhere above, the sky must be turning orange, pink, violet—those old heavenly bruises spreading over the river of air.

And I, who have no eyes, see fish flashing in a pail.

I, who have no mouth, ask again whether there is heaven.

No one answers but the worms, tender and tireless, speaking in the language of return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
